title: Non-Small Cell Lung Carcinoma With Bilayered Architecture and TP53 Alteration: A Diagnostic Pitfall and a Potential Distinct Entity.
authors: Liu Y, Zhang B, Cui X et al.
abstract: The presence of a continuous basal cell layer is generally regarded as a defining feature of bronchiolar adenoma/ciliated muconodular papillary tumor (BA/CMPT), and preservation of this bilayered architecture is commonly used as a surrogate marker of benign behavior. We report a 1.1-cm pulmonary nodule detected in a 75-year-old never-smoker that exhibited marked high-grade cytologic atypia in both luminal and basal cells. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated diffuse strong P53 expression and an increased proliferative index (Ki-67 approximately 10%). Targeted next-generation sequencing revealed a pathogenic TP53 mutation (p.A161T). Despite the intact basal layer, the diffuse high-grade cytology and shared strong P53 expression in both compartments indicate that this lesion represents a fully malignant carcinoma rather than a benign BA/CMPT. In practice, it can only be classified as non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), NOS, with a distinctive bilayered phenotype. This case emphasizes that a preserved basal cell layer does not always equate to benignity, and it highlights a rare tumor type that may mimic BA/CMPT, carrying a risk of underdiagnosis. Integrating cytology, immunophenotype, and molecular findings is crucial for correct classification.

title: Screening opportunity gap in COPD evaluation after low-dose CT findings: implications for risk-based spirometry in primary care.
authors: Hotta T, Nakao M, Shimizu S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Low-dose chest computed tomography (CT) frequently detects findings suggestive of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). However, the pathway from CT detection to physiological confirmation remains poorly characterized in real-world clinical practice. This study evaluated follow-up pathways after CT findings suggestive of COPD and assessed whether simple clinical factors could identify individuals at high risk of airflow limitation.
METHODS: This retrospective observational study analyzed data from a voluntary, self-paid, community-based low-dose chest CT screening program in Japan that was open regardless of age or smoking history. Among 34,425 examinations conducted from fiscal year 2015 through February 2025, 1,336 examinations referred for suspected COPD were analyzed. Follow-up pathways were categorized as no documented follow-up, follow-up without spirometry, and follow-up with spirometry. Two multivariable logistic regression models evaluated documented follow-up and spirometry use. Airflow limitation was defined as a post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC ratio < 0.70.
RESULTS: Among 1,336 examinations, 305 (22.8%) had no documented follow-up, 556 (41.6%) had documented follow-up without spirometry, and 475 (35.6%) had documented follow-up with spirometry. Among those who underwent spirometry, airflow limitation was identified in 298 (62.7%). Current smoking was associated with lower documented follow-up, whereas older age and greater cumulative smoking exposure were associated with spirometry use. Concurrent suspicion of lung cancer was associated with a lower likelihood of spirometry use. Airflow limitation rates increased according to simple clinical risk factors. Examinations with all three risk factors-age ≥ 70 years, pack-years ≥ 40, and respiratory symptoms-had an airflow limitation prevalence of 79.8%. Notably, 90 examinations without spirometry met these high-risk criteria.
CONCLUSION: In this community-based CT screening program, substantial gaps were observed in documented follow-up after referral for suspected COPD and subsequent spirometry use despite the high prevalence of airflow limitation among those tested. Simple clinical factors may help identify high-risk individuals and improve targeted spirometry use in routine clinical practice.

title: History of Smoking and Prognosis of Patients With Non-small Cell Lung Cancer.
authors: Svaton M, Domecky P, Venclicek O et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/AIM: Smoking is a known risk factor for the development of non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, conflicting results are reported in the literature regarding the risk of smoking on the prognosis of patients with NSCLC. Moreover, these studies were often conducted before the era of personalized targeted therapy and immunotherapy, which can significantly improve the prognosis of patients. The aim of the present study was to evaluate the prognosis of patients with NSCLC in relation to their smoking history.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: This retrospective multicentre study included all patients from the Czech LUCAS registry with baseline tumour characteristics. Overall survival was assessed using Kaplan-Meier estimates, with differences between groups evaluated by the log-rank test and multivariate Cox regression model, adjusting for covariates and stratifying by disease stage when proportional hazards assumptions were violated.
RESULTS: A total of 3,372 patients were included. In the univariate model, non-smokers had a significantly better prognosis than former and current heavy smokers (with a history of ≥40 pack-years), hazard ratio=1.19 (95% confidence interval=1.01-1.42), p=0.043; and hazard ratio 1.19 (95% confidence interval=0.03-1.37), p=0.018, respectively. This relationship was not significant in the multivariate model. The absence of a prognostic significance of smoking at the time of NSCLC diagnosis was also demonstrated in a multivariate model both in patients with advanced disease treated with anticancer drugs and in patients who underwent surgery.
CONCLUSION: Although smoking/ex-smoking at the time of NSCLC diagnosis had a negative prognostic impact in univariate analysis, multivariate analysis did not demonstrate smoking itself as an independent prognostic factor for NSCLC. Therefore, other factors, including poorer performance status, likely contributed to the poorer outcome for smokers.

title: Development and validation of a model using thoracic vertebrae data from low-dose CT scans for detecting AI-QCT-defined lumbar osteoporosis.
authors: Zhang Y, Rong C, Zhang Y et al.
abstract: Despite evidence supporting opportunistic lumbar osteoporosis screening with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT), a clinically deployable screening strategy is lacking. This study aimed to develop and validate a model using thoracic bone mineral density (BMD) from LDCT for opportunistic screening. This multi-center, cross-sectional study included 18,298 adults who underwent LDCT with coverage from T1 to L2 at 134 Chinese health check-up centers. Outcome was defined as "artificial intelligence quantitative computed tomography (AI-QCT) defined lumbar osteoporosis" based on a mean L1-L2 BMD < 80 mg/cm3 by phantom-less AI-QCT system. Five machine learning models were trained on T1-T12 BMD (n = 11,065) and evaluated internally (n = 4743) and externally (n = 2490). Performance metrics included accuracy, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, Brier score, F1 score and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC). AI-QCT-defined lumbar osteoporosis was present in 1730 (9.5%) participants. Higher thoracic BMD was inversely associated with the AI-QCT-defined lumbar osteoporosis. T12 exhibited the strongest association: each 1 mg/cm3 increment reduced odds by 21.9% (OR: 0.781, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.769, 0.793, P < 0.001). Logistic regression was selected as the final model. In external validation, it achieved an AUC of 0.993 (95% CI: 0.991, 0.996), AUPRC of 0.922 (95% CI: 0.887, 0.951), F1 score (0.813), sensitivity (0.975), and specificity (0.963). AI-QCT-derived thoracic BMD showed potential for identifying AI-QCT-defined lumbar osteoporosis. Integrating phantomless AI-QCT into lung cancer screening may enable large-scale opportunistic screening, but prospective validation against independent standards is required.

title: Don't discard the supernatant: pleural fluid cfDNA for molecular profiling in lung cancer.
authors: Porcel JM
abstract: Pleural fluid supernatant cfDNA should be routinely preserved and can already be used selectively for molecular profiling in NSCLC, while broader implementation requires prospective clinical validation.

title: Identification of TM4SF1 as a novel tumor-associated antigen in biliary tract cancers targetable by CAR-T cell therapy
summary: Background & Aims: Biliary tract cancers (BTCs) are a rare set of genetically heterogenous and aggressive malignancies associated with delayed presentation and poor prognosis. Thus, there is an unmet clinical need for the development of novel therapeutic strategies. Identification of uniquely expressed cell-surface, tumor-associated antigens (TAAs) holds promise in epithelial tumors more generally, as they can serve as ligands for a variety of therapeutics, including CAR-T cell therapy. However, TAA identification in BTCs has been limited by expression in normal liver tissue. Here, we aim to characterize the cell-surface protein transmembrane 4 L six family member 1 (TM4SF1) as a potential BTC TAA targetable by CAR-T therapy. Methods: TM4SF1 expression in BTC relative to normal hepatic/biliary tissue was characterized at the mRNA level by analyzing TCGA datasets and at the protein level by immunohistochemistry of archival primary BTC tissue. Anti-TM4SF1 CAR-T cells were evaluated through in vitro coculture assays against human-derived BTC cell lines and in a cell line-derived xenograft (CDX) model. Results: We find TM4SF1 is significantly upregulated in BTC relative to normal hepatic/biliary tissue and across BTC anatomical subtypes at the mRNA and protein level. To validate TM4SF1 as a targetable TAA in BTC, we show anti-TM4SF1 CAR-T cells demonstrate robust growth inhibition of BTC cell lines in vitro and significant anti-tumor activity against a CDX in vivo. Conclusions: Together, our data provides support for TM4SF1 as a promising TAA in BTCs that can be used for the rational development of targeted therapeutic modalities, including CAR-T cells, in a patient population with significant unmet need.
